362	
363	\subsection{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)}
364	\label{sec:rrmoa}
365	
366	An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states to forecasts, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. The goal of per-window routing is to select, for each input window, the subset of expert adapters best suited to that window's characteristics, so that a quiet baseline and a volatile spike are handled by different adapter topologies rather than forced through the same head. As shown in the introduction, this fails when the router reads normalized hidden states, because RevIN removes the per-window statistics that distinguish input regimes. \textbf{RR-MoA} avoids this by splitting the information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings $\mathbf{H}$ for the experts, while a separate lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to decide which experts to activate:
367	\begin{equation}
368	\mathbf{Y} = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{T}} \underbrace{\widetilde{w}_j}_{\text{sparse weight}} \cdot \underbrace{\text{Expert}_j(\mathbf{H}_\text{FM})}_{\text{deep embedding branch}},\quad
369	\mathcal{T} = \mathrm{TopK}\!\left(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}),\, k\right),\;\;
370	\widetilde{w} = \mathrm{softmax}_{\mathcal{T}}\!\left(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})\right)
371	\label{eq:rrmoa}
372	\end{equation}
373	where $G_\psi$ is a small Conv1d\,+\,pooling\,+\,linear gate ($\sim$1.1K params) operating directly on the raw time series, and each $\text{Expert}_k$ is a canonical adapter head. Routing is restricted to the Top-$k$ experts with the highest gate logits, so only $k$ of $K$ experts execute per sample. With $K{=}5$, $k{=}2$ we obtain $40\%$ of the dense FLOPs while retaining $63\%$ of the dense MSE gain (\S\ref{sec:topk}). The raw input preserves the temporal statistics (trend, amplitude, volatility) that RevIN strips away, enabling per-sample routing that reflects the physical characteristics of each time series window.
374	
375	\textbf{Expert pool.} We maintain $K{=}5$ topologically distinct expert adapters (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d-pool), identified from structural motifs across ${\sim}1{,}200$ architectures in an LLM-guided search (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}). Architectural diversity is critical: replacing the five distinct heads with five identical experts (same topology, different initialization) degrades MSE by $8$--$15\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}). Pseudocode in Algorithm~\ref{alg:rrmoa} (Appendix~\ref{app:setup}).
376	
377	\section{Experiments}
378	
379	\subsection{Setup}
380	
381	\textbf{Datasets and tasks.} Six LTSF benchmarks (ETTh1/h2/m1/m2~\citep{zhou2021informer}, Weather, Electricity~\citep{godahewa2021monash}) with chronological splits and channel-wise normalization~\citep{nie2023patchtst}. We evaluate forecasting ($H{=}96$) and imputation ($20\%$ masked).
382	
383	\textbf{Backbones.} Five backbones spanning two normalization families: instance-normalized MOMENT-small/large~\citep{goswami2024moment} (internal RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin}); LayerNorm-only Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} and Moirai-MoE; and Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos} and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl} as no-instance-normalization negative controls (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}). MOMENT-small is primary. Primary results use a strictly frozen backbone; freeze-level ablations follow.
384	
385	\textbf{Baselines.} Seven baselines: three fixed adapters, LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora} (108-run sweep; Appendix~\ref{app:lora_sweep}), TRACE~\citep{li2025trace}, an independent ensemble of 5 experts, AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} (hidden-state MoE), full fine-tuning (all blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs), and a from-scratch DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} calibration anchor.
386	
387	\textbf{Training and reproducibility.} Adam, MSE loss, 15 epochs; 5 seeds for the core grid, 3 for ablations. Backbone dimensions, full hyperparameters, and per-baseline configurations: Appendix~\ref{app:setup}. All code, raw JSON results, routing-weight logs, and a self-verification script (\texttt{verify.py}) that re-derives every numerical claim from raw data accompany the submission.
388	
389	\subsection{Main Results}
390	\label{sec:main_results}
391	
392	RR-MoA's case rests on three claims: that fixed-topology adapters are suboptimal, that the natural MoE remedy collapses on instance-normalized backbones, and that the collapse cannot be recovered by standard rescue mechanisms. We establish each in turn before comparing RR-MoA against a comprehensive baseline suite.
393	
394	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{RR-MoA vs.\ fixed adapters.} Table~\ref{tab:rrmoa} compares Top-2 RR-MoA against the best fixed adapter, using the \emph{same five expert heads} in all rows. Across 6 datasets $\times$ 3 freeze levels $\times$ 3 seeds $=$ \textbf{54 configurations}, RR-MoA wins every one with tight standard deviations.}
395

RR-MoA wins \textbf{54/54} across 6 datasets (extended grid in Appendix~\ref{app:extended_rrmoa}); the gain is largest when frozen (``Frozen Paradox'').}

1475-\subsection{Statistics Re-Injection Ablation}
1476-\label{app:reinjection}
1477-
1478:A natural counter to RR-MoA is: ``why not re-inject the stripped statistics into the hidden states rather than routing on the full raw signal?'' We test this by replacing the raw-input router with a \emph{hidden-reinjected} router: the gate receives $[\text{mean-pool}(\mathbf{H});\, \mu(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw});\, \sigma(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})]$ (a $d{+}2$-dimensional vector) instead of $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$.

We tested this hypothesis directly by running a pure mixture-of-experts ablation in which the TSFM is removed entirely.

60	
61	\section{Introduction}
62	\label{sec:intro}
63	
64	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide powerful pretrained representations for time series, with several recent variants pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions, and the design of that adapter, more than the backbone choice, determines deployment utility.
65	
66	Today, every public TSFM benchmark uses a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}a)~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, nie2023patchtst, hu2022lora}. Real time series are not so uniform: ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions, and a single adapter topology cannot be optimal for every input window. A natural remedy is a \emph{mixture of expert adapters}: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical: one TSFM in GPU memory can serve thousands of tenants through small ($\sim$1.7\,MB) per-task adapters swapped in microseconds, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).
67	
68	This natural mixture-of-experts approach catastrophically fails on TSFMs that use instance normalization (Figure~\ref{fig:problem_overview}b). When the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}, routing on hidden states with load balancing, is applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to zero in most unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The router learns to send every window to the same expert, and the remaining experts are never used. The mechanism is what we call \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states. Even with the backbone frozen, hidden-state routing still underperforms; with the backbone unfrozen, the dominant expert receives larger gradients which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, closing a co-adaptation feedback loop within tens of training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). The failure is specific to instance normalization: backbones such as Moirai that use LayerNorm instead of RevIN do not collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}). Standard MoE rescue mechanisms (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice) also do not help (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), because the problem lies in the router's \emph{input}, not its optimization.
69	
70	Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is direct. \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen; only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. The same principle predicts a \emph{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning, which we confirm empirically.
71	
72	\paragraph{Contributions.}
73	\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=0.15em, topsep=0.2em]
74	\item We identify \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}, a failure mode of MoE adapters on TSFMs that is distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE-rescue literature, and isolate it through eight converging causal controls.
75	\item We formalize the mechanism through a mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) that yields a signal-ratio predictor of which datasets benefit from raw routing, including boundary cases where they do not, and validate the same principle across three normalization families, five backbones, and a vision modality.
76	\item We propose RR-MoA, a minimal architectural fix that routes on raw pre-normalization input, and a companion variant (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) that restores raw-signal access at the expert level. The non-triviality is not that raw access helps in the abstract, but \emph{which} signal must be restored and \emph{where}: naive $(\mu,\sigma)$ re-injection fails ($+42$--$239\%$ MSE; $11/18$ cells re-collapse), standard rescue mechanisms that do not restore raw access fail ($720$ runs, $\leq 10.9\%$ recovery, $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA), and the signal-ratio predictor correctly flags datasets where raw routing should \emph{not} help (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Together they close the gap to per-dataset supervised baselines while preserving frozen-backbone deployability.
77	\end{itemize}

224	
225	\section{Related Work}
226	
227	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard recipe attaches a lightweight module to a frozen TSFM and tunes it on downstream data: LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}. Recent variations explore multi-scale finetuning~\citep{qiao2025msft}, importance-based LoRA selection~\citep{li2025trace}, input-representation adaptation~\citep{benechehab2025adapts}, structured pruning~\citep{zhao2025prune}, in-context tuning~\citep{faw2025icf}, and PEFT alternatives for Chronos~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora}; benchmarking work includes TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval}. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies} while keeping a single adapter architecture. We instead ask whether the adapter topology should be chosen per input window.
228	
229	\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been used \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale capacity, with experts placed inside the backbone architecture: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. RR-MoA applies MoE on an orthogonal axis, at the \emph{adapter level} on top of a frozen backbone. The two axes are complementary rather than competing: stacking RR-MoA on Moirai-MoE further improves accuracy (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
230	
231	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse is a well-known failure mode addressed by load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}; AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} carries discriminative information. Sweeping the five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN, none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Concurrent work in NLP/vision toward router-free MoEs (AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe}, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe}, Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree}) supports this view: in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}), self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses. \citet{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry; we extend this upstream by identifying what shapes that geometry on TSFMs.
232	
233	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Normalization in Time Series.} RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} mitigates distribution shift; DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts} and Non-stationary Transformers~\citep{liu2022nonstationary} partially recover stripped statistics. Concurrently, \citet{berthelier2026revin} independently show that several RevIN components are redundant or detrimental, and \citet{zou2025ibnorm} argue that variance-centric normalization (BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm) is suboptimal for representation learning because two representations with identical mean and variance can encode different amounts of task-relevant information. We identify a specific, mechanistic consequence of this principle that has not been characterized in the MoE literature: when the stripped statistics carry the \emph{routing} signal in a downstream MoE adapter, instance normalization causes catastrophic routing collapse, a failure mode distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE rescue literature.}
234	
235	\textbf{NAS and LLM-Guided Search.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs; NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} targets vision adapters. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, and ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo} demonstrate LLM-guided program synthesis. We use this paradigm for expert pool construction (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}).
236

> AGENT

Fixed. The blue and red curves are now properly contained within their waveframe boxes in both panels (a) and (b).

**Root cause**: the `\plot[domain=-0.65:0.65]` paths used the raw `\x` value as the global x-coordinate, so curves rendered at x ∈ [-0.65, 0.65] while the waveframe boxes were centered at x = 0.9 (extent [0.175, 1.625]). Only the right tail of each curve overlapped its box.

**Fix**: changed `({\x},...)` → `({\x+0.9},...)` for the blue and red curves in both panel A (lines 114, 117) and panel B (lines 161, 164). Curves now span x ∈ [0.25, 1.55], cleanly inside the [0.175, 1.625] box. Compiles to 44 pages without errors.

Diagnostic: gates fail to learn. We instrumented the per-sample gate mechanism to log its mean
activation per expert per dataset. Across every configuration tested ({rh128, rh192, rh256, rh320,
rh384, rh512} × {d1, d2, d3 raw-branch depth} × {lr, wd, cosine, warmup} hyperparameter
combinations), the learned gates consistently plateau at σ(0.0)≈0.5:

With 15 epochs of training, the gate mechanism extracts no gradient signal about which branch
should dominate because both branches receive co-equal credit for reducing loss from the start. This
is isomorphic to the dual-stream αk ≈ 0.49 observation, indicating it is not a quirk of a single
architecture but a general failure mode of symmetrically-initialized mixture mechanisms on this task.

# Visual Audit: Findings & Fix Plan

I've inspected all 10 figures at high resolution. Below are the issues found and proposed fixes.

## Issues confirmed (need fixing)

### 1. Figure 2 — `fig:framework` (line 240) — routing weight labels misaligned
**Problem:** The `$w_2$` label sits *inside* the "Last Token" box (overlaps the box bottom border), while `$w_4$` sits *below* the "Attention" box. Asymmetric placement looks accidental.
**Source (lines 352–353):**
```latex
\node[font=\scriptsize, text=orange!70, anchor=south] at (8.7, 1.85) {$w_2$};
\node[font=\scriptsize, text=orange!70, anchor=north] at (8.7, -0.55) {$w_4$};
```
**Fix:** Move both labels symmetrically OUTSIDE the boxes (below the orange dashed arrow tip in both cases). Boxes are at y=2.0 (e2) and y=-0.4 (e4); arrows enter at `[yshift=-0.18cm]` ⇒ y=1.82 and y=-0.58. Place both labels just below the arrow tip:
```latex
\node[font=\scriptsize, text=orange!70, anchor=north east] at (8.85, 1.78) {$w_2$};
\node[font=\scriptsize, text=orange!70, anchor=north east] at (8.85, -0.62) {$w_4$};
```

### 2. Figure 5 right — `fig:signal_ratio` (lines 616–624) — overlapping labels at h1/W cluster
**Problem:** Points h1 (x=0.566, y=−43.2) and W (x=0.703, y=−44.6) sit close together. Labels "h1" (anchor=east, x=0.54) and "W" (anchor=east, x=0.67) both project leftward and overlap each other in the rendered scatter; "Sol" sits to the LEFT of its dot while every other low-x label is to the RIGHT, creating an odd visual asymmetry.
**Source (lines 616–621):**
```latex
\node[...anchor=east] at (axis cs:0.04, -32.9) {Sol};
\node[...anchor=west] at (axis cs:0.17, +2.9) {Traf};
\node[...anchor=west] at (axis cs:0.27, -26.8) {Elec};
\node[...anchor=east] at (axis cs:0.54, -43.2) {h1};
\node[...anchor=west] at (axis cs:0.70, -51.1) {m1};
\node[...anchor=east] at (axis cs:0.67, -44.6) {W};
```
**Fix:** Disambiguate the h1/W cluster by pushing one label vertically, and right-anchor "Sol" for visual consistency:
```latex
\node[...anchor=west] at (axis cs:0.08, -32.9) {Sol};       % was anchor=east, x=0.04
\node[...anchor=south] at (axis cs:0.566, -39.5) {h1};      % vertical separation
\node[...anchor=north] at (axis cs:0.703, -47.5) {W};       % vertical separation
```

## Issues observed but considered acceptable (no fix needed)

| Figure | Observation | Why no fix |
|---|---|---|
| F.2 (line 2160) SR-MoA arch | σ_k → Expert arrows visually similar to H → Expert arrows | Two-color scheme (blue stream / orange routing) is consistent with caption legend; dual-arrow-on-same-line is intentional |
| F.3 (`fig:routing_viz`) | conv1d expert barely visible (purple) | Reflects data, not bug; this is the empirical finding (conv1d receives ~0 routing weight) |
| C.1 (`fig:dose_response`) | Some markers at α=0 sit very close in the y-band | Color-encoded legend distinguishes them; faithful to data |

## Issues already resolved
- **Figure 1 (`fig:problem_overview`, lines 79–223):** Curves clipping outside waveframe boxes — fixed earlier in this session by adding `+0.9` x-offset to blue/red plot domains in both panels (lines 113–117 and 160–164). Verified clean in re-render.

## Other figures (clean)
Figures 3 (trajectory, p.6), 4 (causal_contrast, p.7), 6 (`fig:dose_response`, p.17 — same as C.1), F.1 (collapse_mechanism, p.20), Q.1 (residual_ia_arch, p.27) — all visually correct.

## Proposed fix execution
